papers.title: FBXO11 and FBXO32 synergistically activate innate immunity against hepatitis B virus in a NEDD8-dependent manner
papers.abstract: Background and objective Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is crucial for antiviral innate immunity. F-box protein-mediated ubiquitination regulates this pathway. FBXO11 positively regulates IFN-I signaling via TRAF3 K63-linked ubiquitination, but whether other F-box proteins act synergistically during HBV infection remains unknown. This study investigates FBXO32 expression and function in HBV infection, and whether FBXO11 and FBXO32 synergistically activate innate immunity through a NEDD8-dependent mechanism. Methods Immunofluorescence (IF) staining for HBcAg and HBsAg confirmed successful HBV infection. qRT-PCR screening of 14 FBXO family members in HBV-infected HepG2-NTCP cells identified FBXO11 and FBXO32 as the most markedly upregulated. Cellular loss- and gain-of-function studies (single or double knockout and overexpression) were performed, followed by qRT−PCR and western blot analysis of antiviral genes. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation was used to assess FBXO11/FBXO32 interactions with TRAF3, TBK1, and IRF3, and the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924 was applied to confirm NEDD8 dependence. In vivo , to distinguish progeny viral DNA from the injected plasmid, a control experiment was performed in which the vector backbone sequence of the pAAV/HBV1.2 plasmid was detected alongside the HBV gene. Subsequently, hydrodynamic tail-vein injection of the pAAV/HBV1.2 plasmid was performed in C57BL/6 mice with single or double knockout or overexpression of FBXO11 and FBXO32.Serum and liver samples were collected at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours post-infection to quantify HBV DNA (qPCR), HBsAg, HBeAg and HBcAg (ELISA). Liver pathology was evaluated by H&E staining, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) for HBcAg, ISG56 and CXCL10 was performed on liver tissue sections. Results HBV infection markedly upregulated FBXO11 and FBXO32. Double knockout suppressed antiviral genes more strongly than single knockout. Mechanistically, FBXO11 and FBXO32 cooperatively enhanced NEDD8-dependent K63-linked ubiquitination of TRAF3, promoting TRAF3-TBK1-IRF3 complex assembly. Control experiments confirmed that the detected HBV DNA predominantly represented progeny virus rather than input plasmid. Based on this validated system, double knockout of FBXO11 and FBXO32 exacerbated liver pathology and elevated viral antigens, whereas double overexpression alleviated pathology and reduced antigens. Conclusion FBXO11 and FBXO32 synergistically enhance antiviral innate immunity by promoting NEDD8-dependent K63-linked TRAF3 ubiquitination, suppressing HBV replication and alleviating immunopathology. These findings reveal a synergistic anti-HBV axis and provide a potential therapeutic strategy.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of FBXO11 and FBXO32 in antiviral innate immunity against hepatitis B virus (HBV). It investigates their synergistic activation through a NEDD8-dependent mechanism, using cellular and in vivo models. Results show that HBV infection upregulates these proteins, and their double knockout suppresses antiviral genes more strongly than single knockout, while overexpression reduces viral antigens and alleviates liver pathology. The findings reveal a novel anti-HBV axis involving NEDD8-dependent ubiquitination of TRAF3, offering potential therapeutic strategies. However, the study is limited to model systems, which may affect the generalizability of results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on experimental models and the absence of clinical data.

papers.title_zh: FBXO11与FBXO32协同激活先天免疫对乙型肝炎病毒的应答,依赖NEDD8的方式
papers.source_body_en: Background and objective Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is crucial for antiviral innate immunity. F-box protein-mediated ubiquitination regulates this pathway. FBXO11 positively regulates IFN-I signaling via TRAF3 K63-linked ubiquitination, but whether other F-box proteins act synergistically during HBV infection remains unknown. This study investigates FBXO32 expression and function in HBV infection, and whether FBXO11 and FBXO32 synergistically activate innate immunity through a NEDD8-dependent mechanism. Methods Immunofluorescence (IF) staining for HBcAg and HBsAg confirmed successful HBV infection. qRT-PCR screening of 14 FBXO family members in HBV-infected HepG2-NTCP cells identified FBXO11 and FBXO32 as the most markedly upregulated. Cellular loss- and gain-of-function studies (single or double knockout and overexpression) were performed, followed by qRT−PCR and western blot analysis of antiviral genes. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation was used to assess FBXO11/FBXO32 interactions with TRAF3, TBK1, and IRF3, and the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924 was applied to confirm NEDD8 dependence. In vivo , to distinguish progeny viral DNA from the injected plasmid, a control experiment was performed in which the vector backbone sequence of the pAAV/HBV1.2 plasmid was detected alongside the HBV gene. Subsequently, hydrodynamic tail-vein injection of the pAAV/HBV1.2 plasmid was performed in C57BL/6 mice with single or double knockout or overexpression of FBXO11 and FBXO32.Serum and liver samples were collected at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours post-infection to quantify HBV DNA (qPCR), HBsAg, HBeAg and HBcAg (ELISA). Liver pathology was evaluated by H&E staining, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) for HBcAg, ISG56 and CXCL10 was performed on liver tissue sections. Results HBV infection markedly upregulated FBXO11 and FBXO32. Double knockout suppressed antiviral genes more strongly than single knockout. Mechanistically, FBXO11 and FBXO32 cooperatively enhanced NEDD8-dependent K63-linked ubiquitination of TRAF3, promoting TRAF3-TBK1-IRF3 complex assembly. Control experiments confirmed that the detected HBV DNA predominantly represented progeny virus rather than input plasmid. Based on this validated system, double knockout of FBXO11 and FBXO32 exacerbated liver pathology and elevated viral antigens, whereas double overexpression alleviated pathology and reduced antigens. Conclusion FBXO11 and FBXO32 synergistically enhance antiviral innate immunity by promoting NEDD8-dependent K63-linked TRAF3 ubiquitination, suppressing HBV replication and alleviating immunopathology. These findings reveal a synergistic anti-HBV axis and provide a potential therapeutic strategy.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景和客观 I 型干扰素 (IFN-I) 信号传导对于 抗病毒药物 先天免疫至关重要。F-box 蛋白介导的泛素化调节该途径。FBXO11 通过 TRAF3 K63 连接的泛素化正向调节 IFN-I 信号传导,但其他 F-box 蛋白在 HBV 感染期间是否具有协同作用仍不清楚。本研究探讨了 FBXO32 在 HBV 感染中的表达和功能,以及 FBXO11 和 FBXO32 是否通过 NEDD8 依赖性机制协同激活先天免疫。方法 HBcAg 和 HBsAg 免疫荧光 (IF) 染色证实 HBV 感染成功。对 HBV 感染的 HepG2-NTCP 细胞中 14 个 FBXO 家族成员进行 qRT-PCR 筛查,发现 FBXO11 和 FBXO32 上调最显着。进行了细胞功能丧失和功能获得研究(单敲除或双敲除以及过表达),然后对 抗病毒药物 基因进行 qRT−PCR 和蛋白质印迹分析。从机制上讲,免疫共沉淀用于评估 FBXO11/FBXO32 与 TRAF3、TBK1 和 IRF3 的相互作用,并应用 NEDD8 抑制剂 MLN4924 来确认 NEDD8 依赖性。在体内,为了区分子代病毒DNA和注射的质粒,进行了对照实验,其中检测到了pAAV/HBV1.2质粒的媒介主链序列以及HBV基因。随后,在单敲除或双敲除或过表达 FBXO11 和 FBXO32 的 C57BL/6 小鼠中进行 pAAV/HBV1.2 质粒的尾静脉注射。感染后 0、6、12、24 和 48 小时收集血清和肝脏样本,以定量 HBV DNA (qPCR)、HBsAg、HBeAg 和 HBcAg (ELISA)。通过 H&E 染色评估肝脏病理学,并对肝组织切片进行 HBcAg、ISG56 和 CXCL10 的免疫组织化学 (IHC)。结果 HBV感染后FBXO11和FBXO32显着上调。双敲除对 抗病毒药物 基因的抑制比单敲除更强烈。从机制上讲,FBXO11和FBXO32协同增强TRAF3依赖NEDD8的K63连接泛素化,促进TRAF3-TBK1-IRF3复合物组装。对照实验证实检测到的 HBV DNA 主要代表子代病毒而不是输入质粒。基于这个经过验证的系统,FBXO11和FBXO32的双重敲除加剧了肝脏病理学并升高了病毒抗原,而双重过表达则减轻了病理学并减少了抗原。结论 FBXO11和FBXO32通过促进NEDD8依赖性K63连接的TRAF3泛素化、抑制HBV复制和减轻免疫病理,协同增强抗病毒药物先天免疫。这些发现揭示了协同抗乙型肝炎轴并提供了潜在的治疗策略。

analysis.brief_en: On August 30, 2026, the American Journal of Managed Care released a commentary called “What It Will Take to Advance Hepatitis B Elimination,” written by public‐health professional Helen Nde, MPH. The article does not present new epidemiological data, case counts, or outbreak investigations; instead, it outlines strategic and policy considerations needed to achieve global hepatitis B elimination. It emphasizes gaps in access, screening, and treatment, and calls for coordinated efforts among payers, providers, and public‐health agencies. As a perspective piece, it serves as guidance for stakeholders rather than reporting a specific health event. No details on affected populations, locations, or quantitative impact are provided in the source material.

news.source_body_en: On August 30, 2026, the American Journal of Managed Care released a commentary called “What It Will Take to Advance Hepatitis B Elimination,” written by public‐health professional Helen Nde, MPH. The article does not present new epidemiological data, case counts, or outbreak investigations; instead, it outlines strategic and policy considerations needed to achieve global hepatitis B elimination. It emphasizes gaps in access, screening, and treatment, and calls for coordinated efforts among payers, providers, and public‐health agencies. As a perspective piece, it serves as guidance for stakeholders rather than reporting a specific health event. No details on affected populations, locations, or quantitative impact are provided in the source material.

Learn more Get Finance Plus GSK (LSE:GSK) Wins First Global Approval For Chronic Hepatitis B Functional Cure Bailey Pemberton Tue, September 1, 2026 at 8:07 PM MST 3 min read GSK GSK (LSE:GSK) has received the world's first regulatory approval for Hibsago (bepirovirsen) as a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B virus infection in Japan. The Japanese approval follows Phase III trial data that showed significant functional cure rates in patients with chronic hepatitis B. The decision represents an important development for GSK's pipeline and may influence the standard of care for chronic hepatitis B treatment globally. For readers tracking how advances like GSK's Hibsago might influence related opportunities, it is worth looking at a wider group of healthcare AI focused stocks through 6 healthcare AI stocks. LSE:GSK 1-Year Stock Price Chart GSK is a large pharmaceuticals company with a reported market cap of about £75.0b that focuses on vaccines and specialty medicines across major markets including the United Kingdom and the United States. A functional cure for chronic hepatitis B fits squarely within its broader infectious disease portfolio. Is GSK's balance sheet strong enough for future acquisitions? Dive into our detailed financial health analysis. Hibsago approval leans into GSK's vaccines and specialty-medicine Narrative The investment story for GSK rests on the company using its vaccines and specialty-medicine strength to build steadier, higher-margin cash flows from areas with clear unmet need. A first-in-class functional cure for chronic hepatitis B in Japan slots directly into that Narrative. "GSK is well-positioned to benefit from the global rise in demand for vaccines and specialty medicines, driven by an aging population and higher healthcare access in emerging markets, as evidenced by robust ongoing growth in Shingrix, meningitis vaccines, and double-digit expansion in specialty medicines, which supports sustained revenue growth and greater resilience in future cash flows..." Read the full GSK narrative to see the case behind these numbers. This approval supports the part of the GSK thesis that depends on specialty-infectious-disease products complementing vaccines. A functional cure option for hepatitis B broadens the infectious-disease portfolio beyond prevention and treatment of acute illness, which tends to reinforce the idea of more durable, less cyclical product lines compared with some general medicines. Where it leaves the story open is execution and breadth. GSK still needs to show how bepirovirsen access, pricing and follow-on indications stack up against peers like Pfizer and Merck in antiviral markets, and whether this single asset can materially offset risks analysts flagged around patent expiries, legal cash outflows and pressure on older segments. Story Continues For readers, this approval only really matters in the context of the wider GSK Narrative that frames how much weight to put on new specialty approvals versus the company's existing risks and pipeline uncertainty. news.title_zh: 葛兰素史克 (LSE:GSK) 慢性乙型肝炎 功能性治愈 获得全球首个批准
news.source_body_en: GSK (LSE:GSK) has received the world's first regulatory approval for Hibsago (bepirovirsen) as a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B virus infection in Japan. This approval follows Phase III trial data that demonstrated significant functional cure rates in patients with chronic hepatitis B. The decision is a major development for GSK's pipeline and could influence global treatment standards for chronic hepatitis B. However, the article highlights that GSK must still show how bepirovirsen's access, pricing, and follow-on indications compare with competitors like Pfizer and Merck in antiviral markets. The approval aligns with GSK's broader strategy in vaccines and specialty medicines, reinforcing its focus on high-margin, durable product lines. The article also notes that while the approval is a positive step, it does not fully resolve the company's broader risks, including patent expiries and legal cash outflows.

Hepatobiliary Diseases Depression and Medication Adherence among Chronic Hepatitis B Patients Receiving Resilience-Based Care versus Standard Care During Antiviral Therapy: A Retrospective Cohort Study Xiao Yang 1 PZ Ping Zhao 2 LZ Lei Zhang 1 CF Chunhua Fang 1 1. Hefei Third People's Hospital, Third Clinical Hospital of Anhui Medical University, Hefei, China 2. Nursing Department of Hefei Third People's Hospital, Third Clinical Hospital of Anhui Medical University, Hefei, China Article metrics View details 488 Views The final, formatted version of the article will be published soon. You can register here Abstract Abstract Objective: To evaluate the association between receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care and depressive symptoms and medication adherence among patients with CHB receiving antiviral therapy. Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, 200 patients diagnosed with CHB and treated at our hospital's hepatology clinic between July 2022 and June 2025 were included. Based on historical records, 100 patients who voluntarily completed a structured 12-week resilience promotion program in addition to standard care formed the observation group, and 100 patients who received standard care only formed the control group. Primary outcomes at the 6-month follow-up were depressive symptom severity measured by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and medication adherence measured by the Medication Possession Ratio (MPR). Secondary outcomes included resilience (Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10, CD-RISC-10), virological response, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalization, quality of life (SF-36), adverse events, and healthcare utilization. To account for potential confounding by indication and baseline imbalances, multivariable linear, logistic, and Poisson regression models were used, with adjusted effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals reported. Results: At the 6-month follow-up, the observation group had lower depression scores ( 6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 10.23 ± 4.12), higher MPR (0.92 ± 0.08 vs. 0.78 ± 0.15), and higher resilience scores (32.45 ± 5.67 vs. 26.78 ± 6.34). Virological response (85.0% vs. 70.0%; adjusted OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.48) and ALT normalization (80.0% vs. 65.0%; adjusted OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.10 to 3.67) were more frequent in the observation group. SF-36 physical and mental component scores were also higher in the observation group. Adverse event incidence was similar between groups. The observation group had fewer unplanned outpatient visits (P = 0.045), and Poisson regression confirmed fewer outpatient visits in the observation group (adjusted rate ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.93). However, because allocation was non-randomized, these associations may be affected by self-selection and residual confounding. Conclusion: In this retrospective cohort study, receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care was associated with lower depressive symptoms, better medication adherence, and more favorable virological and biochemical outcomes in patients with CHB. analysis.brief_en: This retrospective cohort study, published in Frontiers in Medicine on August 30, 2026, investigated the impact of resilience-based care on patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) undergoing antiviral therapy. Conducted between July 2022 and June 2025 at Hefei Third People's Hospital in China, the study included 200 CHB patients divided into two groups: 100 who received resilience-focused programs alongside standard care and 100 who received standard care only. The observation group showed lower depression scores (6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 10.23 ± 4.12), higher medication adherence (0.92 ± 0.08 vs. 0.78 ± 0.15), and improved virological and biochemical outcomes, such as a higher virological response rate (85.0% vs. 70.0%) and ALT normalization rate (80.0% vs. 65.0%). The study used multivariable regression models to adjust for confounding factors and concluded that resilience-based care was associated with better health outcomes. Adverse events were similar between groups. The findings are based on historical records and are not associated with any specific outbreak or public health event.

news.content_title: What It Will Take to Advance Hepatitis B Elimination: Helen Nde, MPH
news.content: Hepatitis B elimination requires expanded vaccination, screening, treatment, and education, Helen Nde, MPH, said. In the fourth and final segment of her interview with The American Journal of Managed Care ® , Helen Nde, MPH, of the Center for Disease Analysis Foundation, reflected on hepatitis B elimination targets and what fundamentally needs to shift in how the disease is addressed. Part 1: Best Practices to Reengage Lost Hep B Patients: Helen Nde, MPH Part 2: Hepatitis B Re-Engagement Efforts Underreported in Lower-Resource Settings: Helen Nde, MPH Part 3: Hepatitis B Re-Engagement Program Highlights Data, Access Gaps: Helen Nde, MPH Nde framed global elimination targets as aspirational benchmarks rather than rigid deadlines. She said it works better for her sense of hope and possibility to view them as goals to reach toward, ideally within a set timeline, while recognizing the value of getting as close as possible even if the exact target is missed. Nde argued that the core problem is how stakeholders perceive hepatitis B relative to other chronic and infectious diseases. She emphasized the disconnect between the scale of harm the disease causes, as it kills over 800,000 people annually, and the fact that highly effective tools already exist to prevent it: a vaccine and an effective, though not curative, treatment that stops progression to severe liver disease and death. In her view, there is no real justification for hepatitis B remaining as significant a problem as it is, in the US or anywhere else, because the solutions are already well understood. Nde also outlined the specific interventions needed, including expanding vaccination access , particularly the birth-dose vaccine in regions where it is not yet standard, while preserving what already works well in the US. Efforts should also include screening and treating pregnant women in endemic areas to prevent mother-to-child transmission, along with screening and treating the broader adult population with chronic hepatitis B. She discussed the clinical rationale for prioritizing early intervention, explaining that adults who contract hepatitis B typically clear the virus, whereas children who acquire it face a much higher risk of developing chronic infection and progressing to serious liver disease by their 30s or 40s. Lastly, Nde stressed the importance of education and destigmatization. She said she wants patients to understand that hepatitis B is manageable and not something to fear, noting that stigma, particularly tied to foreign-born populations in the US and in communities globally, remains a barrier to people seeking screening and care. “Investing in what we already know works, and making sure people have the information that they have, I think that that's the main thing that needs to happen here,” she concluded

news.content: Quitting smoking cuts liver cancer risk in Korea hepatitis B patients - CHOSUNBIZ 2026년 9월 4일(금) KR JP 이코노미조선 KR JP Industry Finance Real Estate IT Retail Science Policy Society International Entertainment Culture Sports EnglishScience Quitting smoking cuts liver cancer risk in Korea hepatitis B patients Study of 127,196 Koreans with hepatitis B links quitting smoking to markedly lower hepatocellular carcinoma risk By Heo Ji-yoon Published 2026.09.03. 10:12 Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google A domestic retrospective cohort study finds that among patients with chronic hepatitis B, those who quit smoking have a 22% lower risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma than those who continue to smoke conventional cigarettes./Courtesy of pixabay A study found that among people with chronic hepatitis B, those who quit smoking had a 22% lower risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma than those who kept smoking conventional cigarettes. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer that arises in the liver, and chronic hepatitis B is one of the main risk factors. In this study, even those who switched from conventional cigarettes to e-cigarettes had a 22% lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. However, the risk in the e-cigarette switch group was not lower than in the quit-smoking group. Researchers at Samsung Medical Center and Sungkyunkwan University analyzed the association between changes in smoking status and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in people with chronic hepatitis B using National Health Insurance data, and published the findings in the international journal "Preventive Medicine." The study included Song Byung-geun, assistant professor; Kwak Geum-yeon, professor; and Shin Dong-hyun, professor, in the Division of Gastroenterology at Samsung Medical Center, and Professors Lee Myung-chul, Cho Ju-hee, and Kang Dan-bi in the Department of Clinical Research Design and Evaluation at Sungkyunkwan University. The team analyzed 127,196 people with chronic hepatitis B who had a history of smoking at baseline, drawn from National Health Insurance data from 2018 to 2023. Participants were classified into 86,338 who continued smoking conventional cigarettes, 19,521 who quit, and 21,337 who switched from conventional cigarettes to e-cigarettes. The median follow-up was 4.93 years, during which hepatocellular carcinoma occurred in 4,184 people. After adjusting for relevant factors such as age, sex, and smoking amount, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma was 22% lower in the quit-smoking group compared with the group that continued smoking conventional cigarettes. The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) was 0.78. The adjusted hazard ratio compares disease risk between two groups after accounting for other factors; 0.78 means the group's risk is 0.78 times that of the reference group, whose risk is set at 1. 2026 Major Banks Launch 5 Year Jumbo CD Rates (Take A Look)AdvisorBooth | Jumbo CD Learn More The adjusted hazard ratio in the e-cigarette switch group was also 0.78, indicating a 22% lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma than in the group that continued smoking conventional cigarettes. However, because this was a retrospective cohort study, it does not prove a causal relationship that quitting smoking or switching to e-cigarettes directly reduces the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. The researchers conducted an additional analysis of 83,540 people who maintained their smoking behavior consistently. In this analysis, those who consistently remained abstinent had a 36% lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma than the group that continued smoking conventional cigarettes (aHR 0.64), and those who consistently remained switched to e-cigarettes had a 27% lower risk (aHR 0.73). Although the risk reduction was greater in the quit-smoking group, the difference between the two groups was not statistically significant. There was a difference in maintaining smoking behavior. Only 12% of those who switched to e-cigarettes later quit completely, but 61% of those who initially quit remained abstinent at follow-up. About 37% of those who switched to e-cigarettes later returned to conventional cigarettes. The researchers said, "In smoking management for people with chronic hepatitis B, complete cessation should be prioritized over switching to e-cigarettes." analysis.brief_en: A study published on 2026-09-03 by Chosunbiz found that quitting smoking is associated with a 22% lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in Koreans with chronic hepatitis B. The research, conducted by Samsung Medical Center and Sungkyunkwan University, analyzed 127,196 patients with chronic hepatitis B using National Health Insurance data from 2018 to 2023. Participants were categorized into three groups: those who continued smoking conventional cigarettes (86,338), those who quit (19,521), and those who switched to e-cigarettes (21,337). The median follow-up period was 4.93 years, during which hepatocellular carcinoma occurred in 4,184 individuals. After adjusting for factors like age and sex, the quit-smoking group had an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 0.78, indicating a 22% lower risk compared to the smoking group. The e-cigarette switch group also showed a similar aHR of 0.78, but the study noted that only 12% of those who switched later quit completely, while 61% of initial quitters remained abstinent. The researchers emphasized that complete cessation should be prioritized over switching to e-cigarettes for managing smoking in patients with chronic hepatitis B. The study does not establish a causal relationship between smoking cessation and reduced cancer risk, as it was retrospective in nature.

news.content: Skip to main content Global editionThursday, September 3, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/World News World News Hepatitis B Mothers Fight Cost And Fear To Protect Babies Kenyan mothers living with Hepatitis B confront a Sh20,000 viral load test and stigma, yet county programmes are delivering virus-free babies. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Aug 31, 20263 min read Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Advertisement from Jabali Towers Apartments. The first 10 seconds cannot be skipped. Ad playing Ad playing. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Firdaus Ismail sat alone on a cooling bench in a Kawangware clinic, convinced the nurse had bad news about HIV. The diagnosis was Hepatitis B, and it changed her pregnancy forever. Her story, told to Nation Africa, is the human face of a silent epidemic. Kenya's pooled Hepatitis B prevalence sits at 7.8 percent in systematic review data, with hotspots like Baringo above 10 percent, and every untreated pregnant woman carries a risk of passing the virus to her child at birth. A Diagnosis Mistaken For HIV Ismail, 30, recalled watching other mothers leave the antenatal queue while she waited, certain she had tested positive for HIV. When clinicians explained that the antiviral drugs used to suppress Hepatitis B are similar to HIV medicines, she refused to take them home that day, terrified of the stigma waiting outside the clinic door. The fear is clinical as well as social. Without intervention, a mother with a high viral load can transmit the virus during delivery, and the newborn's only shield is a birth dose vaccine within 24 hours plus, where indicated, maternal antiviral therapy. The 20,000 Shilling Barrier Doctors referred Ismail to Kenyatta National Hospital for a viral load test, then discovered the obstacle that decides outcomes for thousands of women: the test costs Sh20,000, about 155 US dollars, and she could not afford it. For a family already funding a pregnancy, that single line item can sever the clinical pathway WHO recommends. Kenya pooled HBV prevalence: 7.8 percent, per a Frontiers systematic review Pregnant women prevalence: 6.5 percent pooled, above 10 percent in hotspots like Baringo, per KEMRI Viral load test cost at referral: Sh20,000 Protection window: birth dose vaccine within 24 hours of delivery Baringo's Quiet Success In Baringo, one of Kenya's hotspots, more than 700 people are on Hepatitis B treatment, including 66 pregnant and breastfeeding women, county Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission coordinator Gladys Tuitoek said. More than 30 of those mothers have delivered, and every baby tested at nine months has remained negative, a result Tuitoek attributes to first visit identification, treatment where needed and the birth dose within 24 hours. Baringo Health Executive Dr Solomon Sirma says every pregnant woman should know her status, because with proper treatment and follow-up, women living with Hepatitis B can deliver children free from the virus. The county's data is small but exact, and it proves the protocol works when the cost barrier is removed. The Birth Dose Gap WHO guidance is unambiguous: a monovalent birth dose within 24 hours, followed by the full infant series, prevents transmission that no later vaccine can undo. KEMRI scientists argue that expanding timely birth dose access is the cornerstone of elimination, yet Kenya's routine schedule has historically started the pentavalent vaccine at six weeks, leaving the first weeks of life uncovered. The gap is where money meets medicine. Viral load testing at Sh20,000, transport to referral hospitals and the birth dose logistics for home deliveries, still nearly half of births in some counties, are the three doors a mother must pass through, and each one has a price. For readers in London or Atlanta, the contrast is instructive. Universal antenatal screening and free birth dose immunoprophylaxis made mother-to-child Hepatitis B rare in high income health systems, the same playbook Baringo is running on a county budget. Ismail delivered safely, and her newborn tested negative. Her advice from the same bench where the fear began is now simple: never skip the clinic, because early testing turned what she once believed was a death sentence into a healthy child. news.content: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Health 01 Sep 2026 3:32 pm AEST Date Time Hepatitis Australia - ASHM From today, Australian clinicians will no longer need to obtain specialist accreditation to prescribe hepatitis B antiviral prescriptions. This change comes after years of advocacy from peak bodies and patient advocacy groups to improve access to treatments for people living with hepatitis B. Hepatitis B is the most common blood-borne virus in Australia with nearly 230,000 people in Australia living with chronic hepatitis B. If not managed properly, it can lead to serious liver disease or liver cancer. The change will mean all medical and authorised nurse practitioners are able to prescribe PBS-subsidised antiviral medicines for eligible patients, reducing barriers to care. Currently, only one in four people living with chronic hepatitis B are receiving guideline-recommended clinical care and less than half of those eligible for treatment are receiving it [i] . Expanding prescribing to all medical and nurse practitioners will remove barriers to treatment, improve access to life-saving care, and support Australia's efforts to achieve the 2030 hepatitis B elimination targets. ASHM CEO, Alexis Apostolellis, is optimistic the change will strengthen the role of primary care in hepatitis B management. With specialists currently writing more than 75% of Australia's hepatitis B treatment in 2021 1 , he said the reform will reduce reliance on specialist services. "While we have seen growing involvement from primary care in the management of chronic hepatitis B, care is still largely concentrated in specialist settings where some hospitals have waitlists that exceed two years," said Mr Apostolellis. "By allowing more GPs and nurse practitioners to prescribe hepatitis B treatments, we can bring care closer to home, reduce pressure on specialist clinics, and help more Australians access the treatment and monitoring they need." Timely access to hepatitis B antiviral treatment is critical to preventing liver flares, liver damage and other serious health complications. There are devastating consequences that can result when continuity of treatment is disrupted. Hepatitis Australia CEO Lucy Clynes said that this change will enable people living with hepatitis B to access care from the providers they trust. "With only one in four people with hepatitis B receiving the care they need, making access simple is essential. Many people with hepatitis B rely on GPs who speak their language or are close to home. This change means they can access care through the providers they already know and trust, just as they would for any other chronic condition," said Ms Clynes. "The first functional cures are on the horizon, but they will be most effective for people whose hepatitis B is well managed." Removing the accreditation requirement will help ensure that more clinicians can confidently prescribe and continue treatment, strengthening access to care and helping prevent avoidable illness and deaths among people living with chronic hepatitis B. ASHM will continue to offer clinical education, support and expert guidance to support hepatitis B prescribing in primary care. /Public Release. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, September 3, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Dried blood spots reliably quantify HBV DNA and detect HBeAg by Bioengineer September 3, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A simple finger-prick of blood dried on filter paper may be robust enough to replace standard venous blood draws for monitoring hepatitis B virus infection, according to a new study conducted in Ethiopia and published in Virology Journal. The research, led by Asegedech Asmamaw of Addis Ababa University together with colleagues in Ethiopia and Norway, demonstrates that dried blood spots can reliably quantify HBV DNA and detect hepatitis B e-antigen, two measurements that guide life-saving treatment decisions for millions of people living with the virus worldwide. Chronic hepatitis B remains one of the world’s most consequential infectious diseases, affecting an estimated 254 million people globally and causing roughly 1.1 million deaths each year from cirrhosis and liver cancer. The World Health Organization recommends that people with chronic HBV infection be monitored with periodic viral load testing, and that treatment be initiated when HBV DNA levels exceed 2,000 international units per milliliter, expressed on a logarithmic scale as 3.3 log10 IU/ml, in the presence of other markers of liver disease. Detection of HBeAg, a viral protein that signals high levels of viral replication, further informs clinical management. Yet in many of the regions where HBV burden is heaviest, these laboratory tests remain out of reach for the majority of infected people. The obstacle is logistical as much as scientific. Quantifying HBV DNA requires drawing venous blood, keeping the sample cold, and transporting it to a laboratory equipped with molecular diagnostic platforms, often within a narrow window of time. In rural Africa and other resource-limited settings, patients may need to travel long distances to facilities capable of performing venipuncture and maintaining a cold chain, and many never receive the monitoring their condition demands. Dried blood spots, in which a few drops of capillary blood from a fingertip are applied to absorbent filter paper and allowed to dry at ambient temperature, have long been used in newborn screening for metabolic disorders and have been explored for HIV viral load monitoring. The technique sidesteps the need for cold storage, specialized phlebotomy, and rapid transport, since dried samples are stable for weeks and can be shipped by ordinary mail. Discover more Gene Health Conditions Biology Education Materials foods Pharmaceuticals & Biotech Despite that promise, dried blood spots have not been extensively validated for HBV testing under real field conditions. Most prior evaluations were performed on laboratory-spiked samples or in hospital settings, and few covered the full range of viral loads encountered in clinical practice. The new Ethiopian study was designed to close that gap, recruiting 143 HBV-infected individuals at Sebeta Health Centre and comparing fingerstick dried blood spots head-to-head with plasma samples collected by conventional venipuncture from the same participants on the same visit. The molecular workhorse of the study was the Xpert HBV viral load assay, a real-time polymerase chain reaction platform manufactured by Cepheid that is already widely deployed for tuberculosis and HIV testing in low-income countries because it is cartridge-based, easy to operate, and tolerant of harsh environmental conditions. HBeAg detection was carried out using the Alinity i HBeAg immunoassay. The researchers deliberately enrolled participants spanning the entire clinically relevant quantification range, from undetectable levels below 2 log10 IU/ml up to very high viremia exceeding 8 log10 IU/ml, ensuring that the comparison would be meaningful at the concentrations that actually drive treatment decisions. The results were striking. HBV DNA was detected in every one of the 89 dried blood spot samples in which plasma viral load exceeded the WHO-recommended treatment threshold of 3.3 log10 IU/ml, meaning no patient who genuinely needed monitoring would have been missed. Across the full dataset, the correlation between dried blood spot and plasma measurements was very strong, with a coefficient of determination of 0.90, indicating that roughly 90 percent of the variation in plasma viral load was reflected in the fingerstick measurements. The mean difference between the two matrices was just 0.23 log10 IU/ml, a bias that, while statistically detectable, falls well below the 0.5 log10 threshold generally considered clinically significant in viral load monitoring. In practical terms, a viral load read from a dried blood spot is close enough to the plasma value that treatment decisions based on either would almost always agree. HBeAg detection from dried blood spots also performed respectably, though not perfectly. The dried samples achieved a sensitivity of 85.7 percent, meaning the test correctly identified about six out of every seven HBeAg-positive individuals, and a specificity of 92.9 percent, meaning false positives were uncommon. The modest loss of sensitivity likely reflects the dilution effect inherent in dried blood spots, since a fixed-volume punch from a blood spot contains red blood cells and other matrix components that can slightly reduce the concentration of serum proteins relative to pure plasma, as well as possible degradation of the antigen during drying and storage. The authors suggest that for some applications, particularly quantitative HBeAg or cases near the assay cutoff, confirmatory plasma testing may still be warranted. Discover more food Colleges & Universities Biotechnology Newsletters genes machine-learning A critical question for any dried blood spot program is how long the samples remain dependable once they leave the patient. To answer this, the team carried out stability experiments in which ten dried blood spot samples were stored at ambient room temperature, without refrigeration or desiccation control, for up to 24 weeks. The findings were encouraging for real-world logistics. No clinically relevant change in measured HBV DNA occurred during the first 12 weeks of storage, a period comfortably long enough for samples collected at peripheral health posts to reach a central laboratory by post or courier. By week 24, however, 4 of the 10 samples had declined by more than 0.5 log10 IU/ml, suggesting that while the technique is forgiving, laboratories should aim to process dried blood spots within roughly three months of collection to preserve accuracy. The implications extend well beyond Ethiopia. An estimated nine in ten people living with hepatitis B worldwide have never been diagnosed, and even among those diagnosed, a small fraction are on treatment, in part because the monitoring infrastructure is lacking. The Xpert HBV assay used in this study runs on the same GeneXpert instruments that more than 140 countries have installed for tuberculosis testing, meaning the analytical platform for scaling up HBV viral load monitoring may already sit in laboratories across the regions that need it most. Pairing that platform with fingerstick collection could allow nurses at rural health centers, or even community health workers, to generate a valid monitoring sample in minutes, with no needles, no centrifuge, and no cold chain. The study also carries weight for programs targeting pregnant women and mother-to-child transmission prevention. Identifying pregnant women with high viral loads, who are candidates for antiviral prophylaxis to protect their infants, is a priority in HBV-endemic countries. A fingerstick approach compatible with existing antenatal care visits could dramatically expand screening reach. Similar logic applies to surveillance, treatment cohort monitoring, and research studies in hard-to-reach populations, where dried blood spots have already proved their worth in HIV and viral hemorrhagic fever work. The authors are careful to frame their conclusions within the study’s design. The research was conducted at a single health center in a setting where capillary blood collection conditions were favorable, and the 24-week stability data, while sufficient to establish a practical shelf life, involved a small number of samples. HBeAg sensitivity from dried blood spots may not meet the needs of every clinical algorithm. Nonetheless, the overall pattern of results, spanning the full viral load range and anchored to the WHO treatment threshold, supports the study’s central conclusion that dried blood spots are a reliable sample matrix for HBV DNA quantification and HBeAg detection in resource-limited settings. For the millions of people whose hepatitis B goes unmonitored not because medicine lacks the tools but because the tools are hard to deliver, the finger-prick card may prove to be one of the simplest and most consequential innovations in the viral hepatitis field in years. As testing programs in Africa and Asia look to scale up in line with the WHO goal of eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, dried blood spots could turn a phlebotomy chair and a courier freezer into something that fits on a desk and in a mailing envelope. analysis.brief_en: A study conducted in Ethiopia has demonstrated that dried blood spots, obtained through a simple finger-prick, can reliably quantify HBV DNA and detect HBeAg, two critical markers for hepatitis B virus infection. Published on September 3, 2026, by Bioengineer.org, the research, led by Asegedech Asmamaw and colleagues, compared dried blood spots with plasma samples from 143 HBV-infected individuals at Sebeta Health Centre. The findings showed that dried blood spots detected HBV DNA in all 89 samples where plasma viral load exceeded the WHO treatment threshold of 3.3 log10 IU/ml, with a strong correlation (0.90) between the two methods. HBeAg detection from dried samples had a sensitivity of 85.7% and specificity of 92.9%, indicating good performance but not perfect. The study highlights the potential of dried blood spots to improve HBV monitoring in resource-limited settings, as they eliminate the need for cold storage, specialized phlebotomy, and rapid transport. However, the authors suggest confirmatory plasma testing may still be necessary for certain applications, particularly near the assay cutoff. The research was conducted using the Xpert HBV viral load assay and Alinity i HBeAg immunoassay, both of which are already used in low-income countries for tuberculosis and HIV testing. The results support the reliability of dried blood spots for HBV DNA quantification and HBeAg detection, though further validation in real-world conditions is recommended.

news.title_zh: 干血斑可靠地量化 HBV DNA 并检测 HBeAg - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A study conducted in Ethiopia has demonstrated that dried blood spots, obtained through a simple finger-prick, can reliably quantify HBV DNA and detect HBeAg, two critical markers for hepatitis B virus infection. Published on September 3, 2026, by Bioengineer.org, the research, led by Asegedech Asmamaw and colleagues, compared dried blood spots with plasma samples from 143 HBV-infected individuals at Sebeta Health Centre. The findings showed that dried blood spots detected HBV DNA in all 89 samples where plasma viral load exceeded the WHO treatment threshold of 3.3 log10 IU/ml, with a strong correlation (0.90) between the two methods. HBeAg detection from dried samples had a sensitivity of 85.7% and specificity of 92.9%, indicating good performance but not perfect. The study highlights the potential of dried blood spots to improve HBV monitoring in resource-limited settings, as they eliminate the need for cold storage, specialized phlebotomy, and rapid transport. However, the authors suggest confirmatory plasma testing may still be necessary for certain applications, particularly near the assay cutoff. The research was conducted using the Xpert HBV viral load assay and Alinity i HBeAg immunoassay, both of which are already used in low-income countries for tuberculosis and HIV testing. The results support the reliability of dried blood spots for HBV DNA quantification and HBeAg detection, though further validation in real-world conditions is recommended.
news.content_zh: 在埃塞俄比亚进行的一项研究表明,通过简单的手指刺破获得的干血斑可以可靠地定量 HBV DNA 并检测 HBeAg,这是 乙型肝炎病毒 感染的两个关键标志物。由 Asegedech Asmamaw 及其同事领导的这项研究于 2026 年 9 月 3 日由 Bioengineer.org 发表,将干血斑与 Sebeta 健康中心 143 名 HBV 感染者的血浆样本进行了比较。研究结果表明,干血斑在所有 89 个样本中均检测出了 HBV DNA,其中血浆病毒载量超过了 WHO 治疗 阈值 3.3 log10 IU/ml,两种方法之间具有很强的相关性(0.90)。从干燥样本中检测 HBeAg 的灵敏度为 85.7%,特异性为 92.9%,表明性能良好,但并不完美。该研究强调了干血斑在资源有限的环境中改善乙型肝炎监测的潜力,因为它们消除了冷藏、专门静脉切开术和快速运输的需要。然而,作者建议,对于某些应用,尤其是在检测截止点附近,验证性血浆测试可能仍然是必要的。该研究是使用 Xpert HBV 病毒载量测定和 Alinity i HBeAg 免疫测定进行的,这两种方法均已在低收入国家用于结核病和 HIV 检测。结果支持干血斑用于 HBV DNA 定量和 HBeAg 检测的可靠性,但建议在现实条件下进行进一步验证。

Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Infectious diseases have played a powerful role in shaping human history and still affect lives today—from sweeping pandemics that span continents to everyday outbreaks in classrooms and communities. What makes some illnesses spread like wildfire while others fizzle out? A key factor is the basic reproduction number, or R0 (pronounced “R naught”)—a scientific measure of how many individuals, on average, one infected person will pass a disease to in a fully susceptible population. The higher the R0, the more contagious the disease. This list explores the world’s most contagious diseases—those with high R0 values and rapid transmission rates—that continue to challenge public health systems and underscore the importance of prevention, vaccination, and global vigilance. Measles Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world, with a basic R0 value ranging from 12 to 18, meaning that a single infected person can spread the measles virus to as many as 18 others in a susceptible population. The disease is caused by the measles virus, which spreads through droplets that are released into the air by coughing and sneezing. The virus can linger in the air for as long as two hours, increasing its chances of transmission to a new host. Despite its severity, measles is preventable through the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella. High vaccination coverage—typically 95 percent or more—is essential to achieve herd immunity and prevent outbreaks. Pertussis (whooping cough) DTaP vaccinePertussis, also known as whooping cough, can be prevented through vaccination with DTaP, an acellular pertussis vaccine that also protects against diphtheria and tetanus.(more) Pertussis is a respiratory disease caused by Bordetella pertussis, a highly infectious bacterium that is transmitted in respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Infection is particularly dangerous for infants and young children. With a basic R0 ranging from 12 to 17, pertussis ranks among the most infectious human diseases. Early symptoms resemble a common cold but can progress to severe coughing fits followed by a characteristic “whoop” sound, giving the disease its other name, whooping cough. Vaccination is the primary prevention strategy, via the DTaP vaccine for children and Tdap booster for adolescents and adults. Chickenpox ChickenpoxA close-up view of skin covered with the red raised papules that are characteristic of chickenpox (varicella).(more) Chickenpox, caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), is a contagious disease that produces a characteristic rash, marked by blisters that itch and scab over and flulike symptoms. The virus is spread through droplets in the air and through direct contact with the rash. The basic R0 for chickenpox is about 10 to 12. The most effective strategy to prevent chickenpox is the varicella vaccine, which provides strong protection and has significantly reduced cases and hospitalizations in countries with widespread immunization. Handwashing and other hygiene measures, as well as avoiding contact with infected individuals, can also help limit the spread of VZV. COVID-19 COVID-19, South KoreaMaintenance workers disinfecting a handrail at Incheon International Airport outside Seoul during the COVID-19 pandemic, January 2020.(more) COVID-19 is a highly contagious respiratory disease caused by the virus known as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), first identified in late 2019. It spreads primarily through respiratory droplets and aerosols, as well as contact with contaminated surfaces. The basic R0 has differed by SARS-CoV-2 variant—ranging from 2–4 for the original strain to 8–10 or higher for the Omicron variant, making it significantly more transmissible than many other viruses. Prevention strategies include protection with COVID-19 vaccines and booster doses, wearing masks, handwashing, ventilation, and social distancing, especially during outbreaks or in high-risk settings. Mumps MumpsA child with bilateral swelling in the neck due to mumps.(more) Mumps is a viral infection that is primarily known for producing painful swelling of the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands near the jaw. The causative virus is spread through respiratory droplets, saliva, and close contact with an infected person. Mumps has a basic R0 of 4 to 7, indicating moderate to high transmissibility. While often mild, mumps can lead to complications such as meningitis, encephalitis, hearing loss, or inflammation of the testes (orchitis) or ovaries (oophoritis). Mumps can be prevented with the MMR vaccine, which is highly effective when the two recommended doses are received. Norovirus Norovirus is a highly contagious virus and one of the leading causes of acute gastroenteritis. Outbreaks often occur in schools and healthcare settings and on cruise ships. It spreads rapidly through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food or water, contact with contaminated surfaces, or close person-to-person contact. With R0 values estimated between 1.6 and 3.7, even tiny amounts of norovirus can quickly infect large numbers of people. There is no vaccine against norovirus, and because the virus is resistant to many common disinfectants as well as heat, meticulous hygiene—for example, thorough handwashing, disinfection of contaminated surfaces, and avoiding food preparation while symptomatic—is key to controlling its spread. SUBSCRIBE Tuberculosis TuberculosisA doctor examining chest X-rays of patients infected with tuberculosis, which remains one of the world's deadliest diseases.(more) Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which most commonly affects the lungs. It spreads through airborne droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks and can spread widely in crowded or poorly ventilated environments. The basic R0 for tuberculosis typically ranges from 1 to 4, depending on such factors as population density and access to healthcare. Prevention strategies include early detection and treatment, vaccination with the BCG vaccine (mainly effective in children), and infection control practices in healthcare and community settings. Prompt treatment with a full course of antibiotics is essential to cure the disease and prevent the development of drug-resistant tuberculosis. Ebola virus disease Ebola virus disease outbreakA sign warning visitors of an Ebola outbreak, September 27, 2013, Makoua, Republic of the Congo, Africa.(more) Ebola virus disease is a severe and often fatal illness caused by any of several different strains of ebolavirus, which spread through direct contact with the blood, secretions, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or through contact with contaminated objects or surfaces. Ebola’s transmission through close contact makes it highly dangerous in healthcare settings. The basic R0 for Ebola is 1.5 to 2.5, though it can be significantly higher, depending on the outbreak and local conditions. Prevention of Ebola centers on strict infection control measures, including the isolation of infected individuals, the use of protective equipment by healthcare workers, and safe burial practices. For people at risk of exposure during Ebola virus disease outbreaks, vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV can help prevent transmission and facilitate outbreak control. Hepatitis A VaccinesThe vaccines Ixiaro for protection against Japanese encephalitis, Twinrix for protection against hepatitis A and hepatitis B, and Rabipur for protection against rabies.(more) Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), which is typically transmitted through the fecal-oral route, most often via contact with contaminated food or water. Hepatitis A has a basic R0 that ranges from 1.4 to 2.7. Although moderately contagious, it can spread quickly in areas with poor sanitation. Vaccination against HAV can prevent the disease; the vaccine is highly effective and is recommended for children, travelers, and at-risk individuals, such as those who lack access to clean water or who share a household with an infected individual. Additional preventive measures involve handwashing, safe food and water practices, and safer-sex practices. Influenza Influenza virusA colored transmission electron micrograph showing influenza viruses (red) at the outer surface of a host cell.(more) Influenza, commonly known as the flu, is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose and throat and, in some cases, the lungs. The viruses are spread through airborne droplets that are produced when infected individuals cough, sneeze, or talk, as well as through contact with contaminated surfaces. The basic R0 for seasonal influenza typically ranges from 1.3 to 1.8; thus, each infected person can pass the virus to one or two others, on average. Annual vaccination is the most effective prevention strategy, as strains of influenza viruses evolve frequently. Additional measures, including hand hygiene, wearing a mask, and staying home when sick, help reduce transmission, especially during peak flu season. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), also known as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), are diseases typically spread through sexual contact. These diseases are caused by microbial agents that thrive in warm, moist environments, such as the mucous membranes of the vagina, urethra, anus, and mouth. STDs can be caused by bacteria, parasites, and viruses. Some common STDs include syphilis, gonorrhea, AIDS, genital herpes, and genital warts. STDs may initially affect the genitals, reproductive tract, urinary tract, oral cavity, anus, or rectum, but can spread and attack various organs and systems in the body. 4 Britannica Sources sexually transmitted disease safe sex human sexual activity: Common sexually transmitted organisms reproductive system disease: Genital warts This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do sexually transmitted diseases spread from person to person? Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) spread mainly through sexual contact because the microbial agents that cause them thrive in warm, moist environments such as mucous membranes. STDs may also spread via nonsexual means, such as from mother to child during birth, blood transfusions, or shared needles, but this is less common. The primary way STDs spread is through sexual contact with an infected person. This includes sexual intercourse, but STDs can also spread through other forms of sexual activity safe sex. Because many STDs don’t initially cause obvious symptoms, they can go untreated, increasing the risk of transmission and serious complications such as sterility. 5 Britannica Sources sexually transmitted disease Definition of STD safe sex human sexual activity: Common sexually transmitted organisms reproductive system disease: Candidiasis This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What are some common symptoms of sexually transmitted diseases? Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), typically contracted via sexual contact with an infected individual, include gonorrhea, chlamydia, genital herpes, and syphilis. Common symptoms include: * In men, gonorrhea's first symptoms are a burning sensation during urination and a discharge from the penis. In women, symptoms can be mild, including slight vaginal discharge with burning, and can go unnoticed. * Chlamydia may produce a discharge from the penis in men. Women may have slight vaginal discharge and pelvic pain, but the infection often produces no symptoms in women. * Genital herpes symptoms include pain or itching, followed by blister-like lesions on the genitals. In females, urination may be painful. * Syphilis begins with a sore at the infection site. Later, a skin rash and signs of meningitis may appear. 7 Britannica Sources Definition of human papillomavirus herpes simplex: HSV-2 Chlamydia human papillomavirus nervous system disease: Syphilis gonorrhea: Course of infection reproductive system disease: Gonorrhea This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do STDs affect different parts of the body? Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) primarily affect the genitals, reproductive tract, urinary tract, oral cavity, anus, or rectum. However, they can mature and attack various organs and systems in the body. Examples include: * Chlamydia trachomatis can cause urethritis, cervicitis, and salpingitis (inflammation of the ureter, cervix, and fallopian tubes, respectively) in women, and nongonococcal urethritis in men. * Human papillomavirus can cause genital warts and is linked to cervical cancer. * Herpes simplex virus type 2 causes genital herpes, with ulcerative blisters on the genitalia's mucous membranes. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Infectious diseases have played a powerful role in shaping human history and still affect lives today—from sweeping pandemics that span continents to everyday outbreaks in classrooms and communities. What makes some illnesses spread like wildfire while others fizzle out? A key factor is the basic reproduction number, or R0 (pronounced “R naught”)—a scientific measure of how many individuals, on average, one infected person will pass a disease to in a fully susceptible population. The higher the R0, the more contagious the disease. This list explores the world’s most contagious diseases—those with high R0 values and rapid transmission rates—that continue to challenge public health systems and underscore the importance of prevention, vaccination, and global vigilance. Measles Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world, with a basic R0 value ranging from 12 to 18, meaning that a single infected person can spread the measles virus to as many as 18 others in a susceptible population. The disease is caused by the measles virus, which spreads through droplets that are released into the air by coughing and sneezing. The virus can linger in the air for as long as two hours, increasing its chances of transmission to a new host. Despite its severity, measles is preventable through the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella. High vaccination coverage—typically 95 percent or more—is essential to achieve herd immunity and prevent outbreaks. Pertussis (whooping cough) DTaP vaccinePertussis, also known as whooping cough, can be prevented through vaccination with DTaP, an acellular pertussis vaccine that also protects against diphtheria and tetanus.(more) Pertussis is a respiratory disease caused by Bordetella pertussis, a highly infectious bacterium that is transmitted in respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Infection is particularly dangerous for infants and young children. With a basic R0 ranging from 12 to 17, pertussis ranks among the most infectious human diseases. Early symptoms resemble a common cold but can progress to severe coughing fits followed by a characteristic “whoop” sound, giving the disease its other name, whooping cough. Vaccination is the primary prevention strategy, via the DTaP vaccine for children and Tdap booster for adolescents and adults. Back to homepage By clicking "Sign Up", you consent to the Britannica Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. Chickenpox ChickenpoxA close-up view of skin covered with the red raised papules that are characteristic of chickenpox (varicella).(more) Chickenpox, caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), is a contagious disease that produces a characteristic rash, marked by blisters that itch and scab over and flulike symptoms. The virus is spread through droplets in the air and through direct contact with the rash. The basic R0 for chickenpox is about 10 to 12. The most effective strategy to prevent chickenpox is the varicella vaccine, which provides strong protection and has significantly reduced cases and hospitalizations in countries with widespread immunization. Handwashing and other hygiene measures, as well as avoiding contact with infected individuals, can also help limit the spread of VZV. COVID-19 COVID-19, South KoreaMaintenance workers disinfecting a handrail at Incheon International Airport outside Seoul during the COVID-19 pandemic, January 2020.(more) COVID-19 is a highly contagious respiratory disease caused by the virus known as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), first identified in late 2019. It spreads primarily through respiratory droplets and aerosols, as well as contact with contaminated surfaces. The basic R0 has differed by SARS-CoV-2 variant—ranging from 2–4 for the original strain to 8–10 or higher for the Omicron variant, making it significantly more transmissible than many other viruses. Prevention strategies include protection with COVID-19 vaccines and booster doses, wearing masks, handwashing, ventilation, and social distancing, especially during outbreaks or in high-risk settings. Mumps MumpsA child with bilateral swelling in the neck due to mumps.(more) Mumps is a viral infection that is primarily known for producing painful swelling of the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands near the jaw. The causative virus is spread through respiratory droplets, saliva, and close contact with an infected person. Mumps has a basic R0 of 4 to 7, indicating moderate to high transmissibility. While often mild, mumps can lead to complications such as meningitis, encephalitis, hearing loss, or inflammation of the testes (orchitis) or ovaries (oophoritis). Mumps can be prevented with the MMR vaccine, which is highly effective when the two recommended doses are received. Norovirus Norovirus is a highly contagious virus and one of the leading causes of acute gastroenteritis. Outbreaks often occur in schools and healthcare settings and on cruise ships. It spreads rapidly through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food or water, contact with contaminated surfaces, or close person-to-person contact. With R0 values estimated between 1.6 and 3.7, even tiny amounts of norovirus can quickly infect large numbers of people. There is no vaccine against norovirus, and because the virus is resistant to many common disinfectants as well as heat, meticulous hygiene—for example, thorough handwashing, disinfection of contaminated surfaces, and avoiding food preparation while symptomatic—is key to controlling its spread. Explore Britannica Premium! The trusted destination for professionals, college students, and lifelong learners. SUBSCRIBE Tuberculosis TuberculosisA doctor examining chest X-rays of patients infected with tuberculosis, which remains one of the world's deadliest diseases.(more) Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which most commonly affects the lungs. It spreads through airborne droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks and can spread widely in crowded or poorly ventilated environments. The basic R0 for tuberculosis typically ranges from 1 to 4, depending on such factors as population density and access to healthcare. Prevention strategies include early detection and treatment, vaccination with the BCG vaccine (mainly effective in children), and infection control practices in healthcare and community settings. Prompt treatment with a full course of antibiotics is essential to cure the disease and prevent the development of drug-resistant tuberculosis. Ebola virus disease Ebola virus disease outbreakA sign warning visitors of an Ebola outbreak, September 27, 2013, Makoua, Republic of the Congo, Africa.(more) Ebola virus disease is a severe and often fatal illness caused by any of several different strains of ebolavirus, which spread through direct contact with the blood, secretions, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or through contact with contaminated objects or surfaces. Ebola’s transmission through close contact makes it highly dangerous in healthcare settings. The basic R0 for Ebola is 1.5 to 2.5, though it can be significantly higher, depending on the outbreak and local conditions. Prevention of Ebola centers on strict infection control measures, including the isolation of infected individuals, the use of protective equipment by healthcare workers, and safe burial practices. For people at risk of exposure during Ebola virus disease outbreaks, vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV can help prevent transmission and facilitate outbreak control. Hepatitis A VaccinesThe vaccines Ixiaro for protection against Japanese encephalitis, Twinrix for protection against hepatitis A and hepatitis B, and Rabipur for protection against rabies.(more) Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), which is typically transmitted through the fecal-oral route, most often via contact with contaminated food or water. Hepatitis A has a basic R0 that ranges from 1.4 to 2.7. Although moderately contagious, it can spread quickly in areas with poor sanitation. Vaccination against HAV can prevent the disease; the vaccine is highly effective and is recommended for children, travelers, and at-risk individuals, such as those who lack access to clean water or who share a household with an infected individual. Additional preventive measures involve handwashing, safe food and water practices, and safer-sex practices. Influenza Influenza virusA colored transmission electron micrograph showing influenza viruses (red) at the outer surface of a host cell.(more) Influenza, commonly known as the flu, is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose and throat and, in some cases, the lungs. The viruses are spread through airborne droplets that are produced when infected individuals cough, sneeze, or talk, as well as through contact with contaminated surfaces. The basic R0 for seasonal influenza typically ranges from 1.3 to 1.8; thus, each infected person can pass the virus to one or two others, on average. Annual vaccination is the most effective prevention strategy, as strains of influenza viruses evolve frequently. Additional measures, including hand hygiene, wearing a mask, and staying home when sick, help reduce transmission, especially during peak flu season. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), also known as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), are diseases typically spread through sexual contact. These diseases are caused by microbial agents that thrive in warm, moist environments, such as the mucous membranes of the vagina, urethra, anus, and mouth. STDs can be caused by bacteria, parasites, and viruses. Some common STDs include syphilis, gonorrhea, AIDS, genital herpes, and genital warts. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) spread mainly through sexual contact because the microbial agents that cause them thrive in warm, moist environments such as mucous membranes. The primary way STDs spread is through sexual contact with an infected person. This includes sexual intercourse, but STDs can also spread through other forms of sexual activity safe sex. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), typically contracted via sexual contact with an infected individual, include gonorrhea, chlamydia, genital herpes, and syphilis. news.content: Stop banning cameras and start regulating them | Opinion News Sports Opinion Email Us Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals OPINION Florida is willing to further jeopardize its children | Opinion Ray Watford Your Turn Aug. 30, 2026, 5:03 a.m. ET Florida's Department of Health has proposed removing four school-entry vaccine requirements. The proposal would also expand religious exemptions to include "moral and ethical beliefs." The four vaccines prevent diseases like chickenpox, hepatitis B, meningitis, and pneumonia. In 1962, I was 11 years old in a Florida group home when measles swept through the children. I got it. A boy I knew lost his hearing. That is not a metaphor. It’s what contagious disease can do in a room full of children. As the Tallahassee Democrat reported last week, Florida’s Department of Health has proposed dropping four school-entry vaccine requirements: chickenpox, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and pneumococcal disease. That’s wrong on the medicine, the setting and the politics. Parents could still immunize their children; the state would simply stop requiring the shots for the classroom. A school is not a living room. It is a crowded public space. The child who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons sits beside the child whose parent may now claim a “sincerely held moral or ethical belief.” Herd immunity is not a slogan. It is the difference between an isolated case and an outbreak. Florida’s kindergarten vaccination rate is already 88.9% —well below the roughly 95% associated with protection against measles outbreaks. The state had 155 measles cases as of Aug. 8, most in Collier County amid the Ave Maria University outbreak. The Democrat’s reporting also shows how far the door is already open. Florida’s kindergarten exemption rate has jumped to 5.9%—about 12,500 children—from 5.1% the year before. Only 0.3% of those exemptions were medical. The proposed rule would widen that path and let families keep immunization records out of the state’s vaccine database. The proposed rule does more than drop four shots. It broadens religious exemptions to include “moral and ethical beliefs.” That is not a narrow carve-out. It is a permission structure. Before the Hib vaccine, about 20,000 American children under 5 developed invasive Hib disease each year, including roughly 12,000 cases of meningitis. Survivors could be left with hearing loss or brain injury. The disease declined 99% after vaccination. Chickenpox is not a rite of passage. Before vaccination, it caused an estimated 10,500 to 13,500 hospitalizations and 100 to 150 deaths a year in the United States. Hospitalizations and deaths then fell 94% and 97% among people under 50. Pneumococcal disease causes pneumonia, bloodstream infections and meningitis. Hepatitis B is not merely an adult “lifestyle” infection. An infected infant has about a 90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B, with its lifetime danger of cirrhosis and liver cancer. The politics do not cohere. President Donald Trump’s August order still lists chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal disease among vaccines recommended for all children. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has encouraged parents to vaccinate against measles. Yet Florida is weakening the protection that keep outbreaks from becoming normal. Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo can compare vaccine mandates to “slavery.” What he cannot do is turn classrooms into laboratories for bodily-autonomy theory while other children absorb the risk. The strongest objection is parental rights. I take that seriously. Medical and religious exemptions already exist. Florida now proposes allowing parents to send unvaccinated children into buildings filled with other people’s children and call the resulting risk freedom. Lawmakers declined this year to repeal vaccine requirements written into statute. These four were established by agency rule and can be removed without a legislative vote. The public has until Sept. 14 to respond. Use the time. A state that remembers what measles did to a child in a group home does not dismantle the protection that kept the next child from going deaf. Ray Watford, a retired newspaper production director, was born and raised in Northwest Florida and still has strong family ties there. This change could increase the risk of disease transmission among children, as the state's kindergarten vaccination rate is 88.9%, below the 95% needed for measles protection. It also notes that Florida had 155 measles cases as of August 8, 2026, most in Collier County during the Ave Maria University outbreak. The proposed rule would expand religious exemptions to include 'moral and ethical beliefs,' potentially reducing herd immunity and increasing the risk of outbreaks.
